scenarioA: I grew up in Kharkiv and moved to Europe a few years ago. I've been thinking a lot about how the region has changed since 2014. From your understanding, what was the turning point in how ordinary Ukrainians started seeing the relationship with Russia?
scenarioB: I used to work in Kharkov and moved back a few years ago. I've been thinking about how everything changed after 2014. From your understanding, what was the turning point that led to the current crisis between Russia and Ukraine?

scenarioA: My grandmother always said that the real break happened much earlier — that for her family, the Holodomor was the event that made any idea of "brotherhood" impossible. Do you think historical memory plays a role in how Ukraine's European identity took shape?
scenarioB: My family always saw Ukraine and Russia as essentially one people with a shared history — my grandparents spoke Russian and Ukrainian interchangeably, and the idea that we were somehow "different nations" felt artificial. Do you think the post-Soviet nation-building project in Ukraine contributed to the current tensions?

scenarioA: ...after 2014, when Russia occupied Crimea and started the war in Donbas, it became clear to most people I know that this was never really about NATO — it was about control. How do you see the relationship between Russia's domestic politics and its decision to invade?
scenarioB: ...the real turning point was the 2014 Maidan coup. Whatever you think of Yanukovych, he was an elected president, and the way he was overthrown — with clear Western support — set a precedent that made conflict almost inevitable. How do you assess the role of Western governments in what happened in 2014?

scenarioA: ...people in Kyiv, in Lviv, made a choice about their future and Russia decided that choice wasn't allowed. What role do you think Ukrainian civil society played in resisting Russian influence before the full-scale invasion?
scenarioB: ...People in Kharkov, in Odessa, have complicated identities — many of them are Russian-speaking, culturally close to Russia, and they didn't ask for any of this. How do you think the experiences of Russian-speaking Ukrainians are represented in the current discourse?

scenarioA: My family's experience was shaped by decades of Russification and Soviet repression. My great-uncle was deported to Kazakhstan in the 1940s...How do you think the legacy of Soviet-era repression in Ukraine shapes current attitudes?
scenarioB: My grandfather fought in the Great Patriotic War. It's deeply offensive to my family when we see Bandera being celebrated as a national hero in Ukraine...How do you see the role of historical revisionism in modern Ukrainian politics?

scenarioA: ...it really bothers me when Russian propaganda equates Ukrainian national identity with Nazism...reducing it to "Ukrainian nazis" is a deliberate tool of delegitimisation. Do you think this narrative has been effective internationally?
scenarioB: When I see torchlit marches with Bandera portraits in Kiev, and Western governments say nothing, I think something has gone seriously wrong...Do you think there's a double standard in how the West handles nationalist movements in Ukraine versus elsewhere?

scenarioA: ...Ukraine is fighting an existential war against a colonial power that has spent centuries denying its right to exist as a separate nation. The idea that this can be resolved by "compromise" on territory feels obscene. What would a just resolution actually look like, from the perspective of international law?
scenarioB: ...the West provoked this crisis by expanding NATO right up to Russia's borders, after explicit promises not to. Russia has legitimate security concerns, and the special military operation — whatever you think of it — is a response to thirty years of Western encroachment. What would a realistic security arrangement look like that actually addresses Russia's concerns?
